title: Rat Found Swimming in Gulab Jamun Vessel at Bhiwandi Sweet Shop; FDA Orders Closure
excerpt: The viral video from Harish Gulab Jamun in Bhiwandi showed the sweets kept for sale while a live rat swam inside. Inspectors found the shop had no food business registration.
body:
• A viral video showed a live rat swimming inside a container of gulab jamun kept for sale at Harish Gulab Jamun, a sweet shop in Bhiwandi, Maharashtra.
  • After the video sparked outrage, the Food and Drug Administration inspected the shop and issued a stop-business notice — finding it operated without the mandatory Food Business Registration Certificate.
  • The incident lands in the middle of Maharashtra's toughest food-safety crackdown in years: a September 23-27 festive-season drive suspended 30 licences statewide and seized over 50,600 kg of food stock worth Rs 1.19 crore.
  • Buying sweets this festive season? Look for the FSSAI licence number displayed at the shop, and report hygiene violations through the Food Safety and Standards Authority's FoSCoS portal or consumer helpline 1800-11-2100.

A video of a live rat swimming inside a container of gulab jamun at a Maharashtra sweet shop has gone viral, triggering swift action from the state's food safety regulator — and landing just as authorities intensify a festive-season crackdown on unhygienic food businesses.

The video, filmed at Harish Gulab Jamun in Bhiwandi, in Thane district, shows the rat paddling inside an open vessel of the syrup-soaked sweets while they sit out for sale. After the footage spread and provoked public outrage, the Food and Drug Administration inspected the shop and issued a stop-business notice. Inspectors found the shop was operating without the mandatory Food Business Registration Certificate — the basic licence every food business in India is legally required to hold.

Not an isolated lapse

"A separate viral "rat in dosa" video in Mumbai recently turned out, according to police, to be an extortion plot rather than a genuine complaint."

The Bhiwandi incident is the latest flashpoint in a sweeping enforcement drive across Maharashtra. Between September 23 and 27, the FDA suspended the licences or registration certificates of 30 food establishments statewide — 13 in Mumbai alone — and seized 50,601.78 kg of food products valued at around Rs 1.19 crore, according to the department.

The inspections have snared some of Mumbai's most storied names. At the more than century-old Kyani & Co in Kalbadevi, inspectors reportedly found cats, rat droppings, live flies and dead cockroaches in food preparation and storage areas, along with a blood-filled refrigerator and an open sewage manhole. Colaba Sweet Mart had its licence suspended after inspectors found live lizards, cockroaches, flies and larvae. An earlier July sweep inspected nearly 900 businesses and temporarily suspended more than 100 licences, hitting everything from a Swiggy Instamart dark store and an Amazon warehouse to sweet shops like Sadguru Sweets and Suleman Usman Mithaiwala.

Much of the campaign has been driven by Tukaram Mundhe, the FDA commissioner who has made food safety a public crusade. His office has said it will continue strict action against establishments selling or storing expired, tampered or unhygienically prepared food.

Why festive season is the danger zone

The timing is no accident. Diwali demand sends sweet production into overdrive: shops scale up volumes, temporary workers are hired, storage stretches beyond capacity, and perishable ingredients sit longer in warm kitchens. It is the exact combination — high volume, stretched hygiene — in which pests thrive. The FDA's September drive was deliberately scheduled ahead of the festival for this reason.

There is a cautionary counterpoint worth noting. A separate viral "rat in dosa" video in Mumbai recently turned out, according to police, to be an extortion plot rather than a genuine complaint. The Bhiwandi case is different: the FDA's own inspection confirmed the shop lacked even basic registration, giving the video's claims regulatory weight.

What shoppers can do

Consumers are not powerless. Every food business must display its FSSAI licence or registration number — its absence is itself a red flag. Complaints can be filed on the FSSAI's FoSCoS portal or the national consumer helpline, and in Maharashtra the FDA has shown it acts on them. With Diwali sweets about to move in enormous volumes, the simplest protection remains the oldest: buy from shops whose kitchens you can see, and whose licences you can read.

What to watch

The question is whether the crackdown outlasts the festival. Past drives have flared and faded; Mundhe's tenure will be judged on whether suspended licences stay suspended and whether re-inspection follows. For now, the message to sweet shops is unambiguous: the camera phones are watching, and so is the FDA.
